title: Apple in 1997: How a $1 Billion Loss Became a Comeback
description:
Apple in 1997 lost over $1 billion, its sales had fallen by more than a third in two years, and its debt was rated junk. This case study uses Apple's own 10-K filings to show how the company turned around: the NeXT acquisition and Steve Jobs' return, the $150 million Microsoft deal, cutting the product line, the iMac, a huge inventory cut, and how it set up the iPod and iPhone era. Plus three business lessons you can use: focus, cash runway and cutting complexity.

Apple's fiscal year ends in late September; years in the video are fiscal years. Dollar figures are not adjusted for inflation; US prices roughly doubled between 1997 and 2026. Staff: 1997 = regular employees (excl. 1,739 temporary staff and contractors), 2026 = full-time equivalents. "Under three days" = Apple's fiscal 1997 net loss ($1.045B) / its fiscal 2026 net income per day ($132.2B / 365). The "90 days" line is Steve Jobs' own later recollection (2010), not a figure from Apple's filings. The two-by-two product grid is as described by biographer Walter Isaacson; the four product lines are from Apple's 1999 10-K. The $9,000 runway example is illustrative.

À partir des rapports 10-K d'Apple, on suit le redressement : le rachat de NeXT et le retour de Steve Jobs, l'accord de 150 millions avec Microsoft, la gamme réduite, l'iMac et une énorme baisse des stocks. scenes.say: In nineteen ninety-seven, Apple lost over a billion dollars in a single year. Its sales had fallen by more than a third in two years.

visual.label: Apple's net loss, fiscal 1997
visual.sub: Apple 10-K · sales down 36% in two years

scenes.say: In its latest fiscal year, which ended in September, Apple's profit was about a hundred and thirty-two billion dollars. At that pace, it earns back that whole nineteen ninety-seven loss in under three days.

So how did a company with shrinking sales and junk-rated debt turn around? Using Apple's own filings, we'll walk through the deal with its biggest rival, the products it killed, the computer that brought it back, and the team behind it.
And by the end, you'll see the least glamorous fix in those filings. It freed more than twice as much cash as Microsoft's famous investment.

visual.label: more cash than Microsoft put in

scenes.say: Chapter one. The hole.

Start with sales. In fiscal nineteen ninety-five, Apple sold about eleven billion dollars' worth of products. Two years later, about seven billion. And it kept falling, to under six billion in nineteen ninety-eight.

visual.title: Apple net sales by fiscal year

scenes.say: The losses were huge. Eight hundred and sixteen million dollars in fiscal ninety-six. One point oh four billion in ninety-seven. Nearly one point nine billion dollars gone in two years.
Steve Jobs later said, at a conference in twenty ten, that Apple had been ninety days from going bankrupt. That's his memory, thirteen years on. The filings tell a more precise story.

In September nineteen ninety-six, Apple had about one point seven five billion dollars in cash and short-term investments. A year later, one point four six billion. Down about two hundred and eighty-six million dollars, even after a cash injection we'll get to.

Lenders noticed. In October nineteen ninety-seven, Standard and Poor's cut Apple's debt ratings to B minus and triple C, deep in junk territory. Apple's own filing warned of significant voluntary employee turnover. And its old operating system was falling behind. Back in late nineteen ninety-six, Apple had already gone shopping for a new one.

visual.title: Warning signs, 1997
items: Debt cut to junk (S&P: B− / CCC)

scenes.say: Chapter two. The Next bet.

On December twentieth, nineteen ninety-six, Apple, then run by chief executive Gil Uh-mellio, agreed to buy Next, the company Steve Jobs started after he left Apple. The deal closed in February nineteen ninety-seven.

The headline price was four hundred million dollars. Apple's annual report puts the full cost at four hundred and twenty-seven million: mostly cash to Next's owners, plus stock, options, and paying off Next's debt.

And three hundred and seventy-five million of it was written off straight away, as research still in progress. Add a restructuring charge, and Apple lost seven hundred and eight million dollars in the first three months of nineteen ninety-seven alone.

So what did Apple really buy? People and software. Avie Tevanian came from Next to run software. Jon Rubinstein, a former Next hardware chief, took over hardware. And to be fair to Uh-mellio, his team had already hired finance chief Fred Anderson, and started the cost cuts in nineteen ninety-six.

In July nineteen ninety-seven, Uh-mellio resigned. In September, the board named Jobs interim chief executive, in its words, until a new one was found. But new software takes years. Apple needed help sooner, and it came from its fiercest rival.

visual.label: Steve Jobs, Sept 16, 1997
visual.sub: "until a new CEO is named" · Amelio resigned in July

scenes.say: Chapter three. The rival's lifeline.
August sixth, nineteen ninety-seven. On stage at the Macworld show in Boston, Jobs announced that Microsoft would invest one hundred and fifty million dollars in Apple.

Microsoft bought non-voting shares, so it got no say in running Apple. It promised to keep making Office for the Mac for five years. Apple made Internet Explorer the Mac's default browser. And the two companies cross-licensed their patents.

Here's the surprising part. The cash was small: about a tenth of Apple's cash pile. Apple's own filing calls Microsoft an important developer of Mac software. A five-year promise on Office mattered more than the money.
Not everyone liked it. Maclean's reported that the announcement drew boos and jeers. Jobs told the crowd: We have to let go of the notion that for Apple to win, Microsoft has to lose.

visual.text:
"We have to let go of the notion
that for Apple to win,
Microsoft has to lose."
visual.source: Steve Jobs, Macworld Boston, Aug 6, 1997 (via Maclean's)

scenes.say: The same day, Apple announced a new board. All but two directors were replaced. The money and the promise bought time. What Apple did with that time was cut, hard.
Chapter four. Cutting to four boxes.
Apple's nineteen ninety-eight annual report says it simplified its product line, from about fifteen separate products to three main product families.

Out went the Newton handheld and the eMate. Many printers and monitors went too. And Apple ended the Mac clone business, agreeing to buy Power Computing's Mac license and customer list for about a hundred and ten million dollars, mostly in stock.

visual.title: What Apple cut
visual.label: Newton MessagePad and eMate
visual.sub: plus many printers and monitors · Mac clones (Power Computing, ~$110M)

scenes.say: Jobs' biographer, Walter Isaacson, describes him drawing a simple grid: consumer and pro, desktop and portable. By nineteen ninety-nine, Apple's filing listed four computer lines filling those boxes: iMac, iBook, Power Mac, and PowerBook.

The cuts hit people, too. Apple had about ten thousand nine hundred regular employees in nineteen ninety-six, eight thousand four hundred a year later, and six thousand seven hundred by nineteen ninety-eight. Nearly four in ten jobs, gone in two years.
Fewer products meant every bet had to count. The first big one was a strange-looking, all-in-one computer.
Chapter five. The iMac, and the boring fix.

visual.title: The iMac, and the boring fix

scenes.say: In May nineteen ninety-eight, Apple unveiled the iMac: an all-in-one computer, built for getting online, for twelve hundred and ninety-nine dollars. It went on sale on August fifteenth.
It came from a team. Jony Ive, at Apple since nineteen ninety-two, led the industrial design group that shaped its look. Jon Rubinstein's engineers built the hardware.
In its first quarter on sale, Apple shipped two hundred and seventy-eight thousand iMacs. That was a third of all the Macs it shipped. The next year, it sold about one point eight million.

And Apple was profitable again. After four losing quarters in a row, it made money in every quarter of fiscal ninety-eight. Notice the profits started before the iMac even shipped. Cost cuts came first, helped by a faster Power Mac G3 line launched in late nineteen ninety-seven.

visual.title: Apple quarterly profit, fiscal 1998
visual.note: Power Mac G3 from Q1 · iMac shipped in Q4 (Aug 1998) · Source: Apple 10-K, fiscal 1998

scenes.say: Now the least glamorous fix. Inventory: unsold computers and parts. Apple cut it from four hundred and thirty-seven million dollars to just seventy-eight million in one year. From thirty-one days of supply, to six.

That released about three hundred and fifty-nine million dollars in cash. More than twice what Microsoft invested. Fewer products made it possible, along with standard parts, fewer warehouses, and a new operations chief hired from Compaq in March nineteen ninety-eight: Tim Cook.

By September nineteen ninety-eight, Apple had made three hundred and nine million dollars for the year, and its cash had grown to two point three billion. Apple was alive. But it was still a shrinking computer company. Real growth would come later, built on the software it agreed to buy in nineteen ninety-six.
Chapter six. From iMac to iPhone.

Next's software became the base of Mac O S Ten, released in two thousand one. That same year, Apple introduced the iPod. In January two thousand seven came the iPhone, whose software, the Computer History Museum notes, was built on Mac O S Ten.

Notice the loop. Focus made better products. Better products brought back profit and cash. And that cash paid for bigger, riskier bets, like a music player, and later a phone. Each turn made the next one possible.

Today, the iPhone alone brought in about two hundred and fifty-four billion dollars in fiscal twenty twenty-six. That's over half of Apple's revenue. Services added another hundred and twenty-three billion.

Put the two years side by side. Before inflation, revenue is up nearly sixty-eight times. A billion-dollar loss became a hundred and thirty-two billion dollar profit. And about eight thousand four hundred regular employees became about a hundred and sixty-seven thousand full-time equivalents.

A fair warning about hindsight. None of this was guaranteed in nineteen ninety-eight. Apple's sales were still shrinking that year, and the iPhone was nearly a decade away. The turnaround bought a chance, not a result. So what can you take from it?

visual.label: not a result
visual.sub: the iPhone was nearly a decade away

scenes.say: Chapter seven. The lessons.

Lesson one: focus. Fifteen products became a handful. Saying no freed money, people and attention for the few things that mattered. In your own life, list everything that costs you money or time each month, and cut what doesn't earn its place.

Lesson two: know your runway. That's your cash, divided by what you burn each month. If you have nine thousand dollars saved and three thousand in essential costs each month, your runway is three months. Apple's cash bought it time to fix things. Yours does the same.

Lesson three: complexity costs cash. Once Apple had fewer products, its inventory fell by more than eighty percent. For you, fewer cards, accounts and subscriptions means fewer fees and fewer surprises.
And remember who did it. Uh-mellio's team started the cuts and bought Next. Jobs set the focus. Ive, Rubinstein, Tevanian, Anderson and Cook did much of the work. A turnaround is a team effort.

visual.label: Amelio · Jobs · Ive · Rubinstein · Tevanian · Anderson · Cook
